## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="w11-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Solver</dt><dd>Software that finds the best plan of a model, or proves that none exists; here HiGHS, in well under a second once it has loaded.</dd>
<dt>Checks</dt><dd>Balance, limits, ramps, energy and money: a solver answers the model you wrote, so check it against the world.</dd>
<dt>Shadow price</dt><dd>How much the best cost rises per small extra MWh of demand, away from a kink; $40 in 18 of 24 hours, where the combined-cycle is the marginal plant.</dd>
<dt>Mixed-integer programs</dt><dd>Their solve returns no ordinary shadow prices; prices come from a linear program with the on-or-off choices fixed (lesson <a href="m02-unit-commitment.html">M2</a>).</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · inside the solver</span>Peek inside: the simplex method walks the corners</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>Lesson 10's hour again. The <span class="lx-term" data-term="simplex-method">simplex method</span> starts at a corner and moves along an edge to a neighbouring corner that is never worse, again and again, until no neighbour is cheaper. In a linear program that corner is the best plan overall. On this hour every move is cheaper.</p>
<div id="w11-peek" class="lx-guard"><p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, step through the walk here.</p></div>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Why a mixed-integer solve returns no shadow prices</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Linear program.** As demand changes, the best cost is continuous and piecewise linear: straight pieces joined at kinks. The slope of a piece is the shadow price.
- **Mixed-integer program.** The solver searches over on-or-off choices (an off peaker, or one at 30 MW or more), so it returns no ordinary LP shadow prices. The best cost can also jump when a plant switches on.

| At a 30 MW/h ramp limit | [Linear program]{.lx-term term="linear-program"} | [Mixed-integer program]{.lx-term term="mixed-integer-program"} |
|---|---|---|
| Best cost for the day | \$106,300 | \$107,200 |
| Peaker | 35 MWh, some hours below 30 MW | off all day; more wind and solar curtailed |
| Shadow prices from the solve | one per hour | none |

To price a mixed-integer plan, fix its [unit commitment]{.lx-term term="unit-commitment"} (which plants are on), re-solve the linear program, and read prices *conditional on that commitment*. Lesson [M2](m02-unit-commitment.html) builds that model.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>When a shadow price is not unique</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Away from a kink, the shadow price is the cost change per small extra MWh. At a kink, compare the increase and the decrease separately: any value between them is a valid shadow price.

| Hour | +1 MWh costs | −1 MWh saves | HiGHS reports |
|---|---|---|---|
| 07:00 | \$100 | \$80 | \$80 |
| 09:00 | \$40 | \$20 | \$40 |

- **07:00.** Up: the peaker makes the MWh, since the ramp rule would lift 08:00 and 09:00 too. Down: 07:00 and 08:00 each fall by 1 MWh.
- **09:00.** Up: the combined-cycle. Down: 07:00, 08:00 and 09:00 each fall by 1 MWh (\$120), and the peaker covers 07:00 (−\$100).

Such optima are called degenerate. They are common in real models, so read a single reported price with care.

Each price here is a marginal value under stated assumptions: fixed plant sizes, a linear model, and Prairie Town as an island. It is the merit-order price of [lesson 8](08-merit-order.html) read from a solver, not a forecast of a market price.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="w11-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="opt" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If the solver says ‘optimal’, the model is right.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The sign-error model was ‘optimal’ too, at $52,160. Optimal means best for the model as written; checks tell you whether the model is right.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="price" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The demand rule's shadow price always equals the running cost of a plant that is running.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Where a ramp rule is at its limit it is $0 or $80 here: a change at one hour moves the plan in a neighbouring hour too, and the price counts both.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="local" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “In a linear program, a plan that no small change can improve is the best plan overall.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. A linear program has no ‘local’ best that is not also the global best. That is why you could not beat the solver.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="milp" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A mixed-integer program gives shadow prices just like a linear program.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A mixed-integer solve returns no ordinary shadow prices. Prices need a second step: fix the on-or-off choices, re-solve the linear program, and read prices conditional on them.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="w11">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="five" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">At 19:00 the shadow price of the demand rule is $40/MWh. A new 5 MW load runs for that hour. By about how much does the best cost rise?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$40</li><li data-value="b">$200</li><li data-value="c">$500</li><li data-value="d">$0</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About $200: 5 MWh × $40. A shadow price holds for small changes that leave the same rules <span class="lx-term" data-term="binding-constraint">binding</span> (exactly at their limits).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="check" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A model reports a day's cost far below what you expected. What should you do first?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Celebrate the saving</li><li data-value="b">Run a different solver</li><li data-value="c">Check that supply equals demand every hour with the reported plan</li><li data-value="d">Lower the time limit</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Check the plan against the physics. Another solver would solve the same wrong model just as well.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>Market operators re-solve dispatch models like this one every few minutes: 5 in the western Energy Imbalance Market, as <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=32052">EIA</a> reported in 2017.</p>
<p>Their prices are shadow prices of balance rules, one for each location on the network: lesson <a href="m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html">M1</a>.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">

<li>EIA (2017). <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=32052">The western U.S. sub-hourly wholesale electricity market is expanding</a>. Today in Energy.</li>
